The meeting was called to order by Chair Lopez at 6:18 p.m., in the Norwalk City Hall,
Council Chambers, 12700 Norwalk Boulevard, Norwalk, California. Present were
Commissioner Barragan, Commissioner Garcia, Vice Chair Apodaca, and Chair Lopez.
Commissioner Navas was absent. Also present were John P. Ramirez, Director of
Community Development; Gloria V. Ramirez, Deputy City Attorney; Alex Hamilton,
Interim Development Services Manager; Sophia Tatlyan, Consulting Senior Planner;
Carlos Rojas, Senior Planner; and Ruth Hoffmann, Administrative Secretary.

MEETING MINUTES

The Planning Commission approved the minutes of the Special Meeting of March 13,
2024.

ZONING TEXT AMENDMENT (ZTA) NO. 2024-01
To amend various sections of Title 17 of the Norwalk Municipal Code (NMC) as it
relates to Specific Plan Area No. 1 (SPA 1). Environmental: Consider and find the
project exempt from CEQA pursuant to Section 15061(b)(3) (Common Sense
Exemption). SPA 1 encompasses an area of approximately 20 acres bounded on
the west by Norwalk Boulevard and the Santa Ana Freeway (I-5), to the south by
the Santa Ana Freeway and Dace Street, to the east by Volunteer Avenue and to
the north by Civic Center Drive.

Chair Lopez opened the public hearing.

Staff presented the legal requisites for notice of hearing. Consulting Senior Planner
Tatlyan presented a report stating that this is a City initiated project; that staff intends to
amend various sections of Title 17 as it relates to Specific Plan Area No. 1 (SPA 1); that
SPA 1 was adopted in 1987 by Ordinance No. 1267 which was intended to establish
objectives, policies, regulations and development standards and review criteria for the
implementation of a compatible blend of mutually supporting land uses consisting of a
multi-story hotel, a wide array of professional offices and retail commercial uses,
complementary commercial entertainment uses and residential condominiums; that SPA
1 encompasses approximately twenty acres, bounded on the west by Norwalk Boulevard
and the Santa Ana Freeway, to the south by the Santa Ana Freeway and Dace Street, to
the east by Volunteer Avenue and to the north by Civic Center Drive.

Continuing with her presentation, Ms. Tatlyan shared that the zoning text amendment will
modify SPA 1 through various changes to further advance the objectives in fostering a
compatible combination of commercial, retail and residential uses; that, currently, SPA 1
only allows for one hotel; that the proposal would allow for an additional hotel; that the list
of allowable uses is to be expanded to include billboards, arcades, a bowling alley,
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 2
Minutes of the Special Meeting  June 26, 2024

entertainment venues, and lounges; that, if adopted, this amendment will allow for
potential future uses subject to applicable review requirements set forth in the Specific
Plan, and updating the list of prohibited uses to remove uses that are outdated or
inconsistent with the objective of SPA 1; that the proposed zoning text amendment will
also provide a mechanism and a process for wayfinding signage which usually is located
on prominent entry intersections to or within a shopping center; that, currently, there is no
process for this, but will be allowed through the Director Approval Request (DAR)
process.

Consulting Senior Planner Tatlyan shared that their analysis regarding the project
indicates that SPA 1 is a unique and prominent center; that, with the text amendment, it
will build on the current success of a thriving commercial center and take advantage of
its position in Norwalk by facilitating new opportunities; that, as stated, the text
amendment will allow for a second hotel, provide greater flexibility and allow for additional
development; that the project is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act
(CEQA) pursuant to Section 15061(b)(3) (Common Sense Exemption) as the project does
not involve any construction nor will it have a significant effect on the environment; that
new projects would require an environmental review as the zoning text amendment only
modifies SPA 1 in the Norwalk Municipal Code; and that it is staff’s recommendation that
the Planning Commission adopt Resolution No. 24-02 recommending City Council
approval of Zoning Text Amendment No. 2024-01, and consider and find that the project
is exempt from CEQA pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15061(b)(3).

Jordan Sisson stated that he represents UNITE HERE Local 11, and that he sent the
letter to the Commission referred to by staff. He indicated that, with the Chair’s approval,
he would like to address their concerns with all three items on the agenda; that they
believe that there is a clear project envisioned for the site and not a potential use,
specifically a 121-room Holiday Inn located just south of the DoubleTree Hotel; that the
February 2024 Norwalk Transit Village Draft Environmental Impact Report includes a
Holiday Inn at the Norwalk Entertainment Center at 13111 Sycamore Drive, and a Digital
Billboard, pending resubmittal; that this is clearly within the SPA 1 area; that the four-
page staff report makes no mention of this; that regarding the proposed ordinance,
Section 17.09.110 Permitted Uses, includes the wording “and Parking/Utility Area” which
specifically allows billboards and entertainment venues in addition to the two hotels; that
this is not mentioned in the staff report; that this is concerning under CEQA because
under CEQA the entire project is supposed to be described; that the report does not
specify what sort of exemption the City is requiring; that the City has to demonstrate that
there is no possibility of environmental impacts; that if there is substantial evidence that
there might be an impact, it makes an exemption inapplicable; that this Specific Plan
Amendment was adopted nearly forty years ago; that the staff report does not include
what the CEQA review was or include the Environmental Impact Report; that they don’t
really know if two hotels were allowed or if entertainment uses were ever envisioned forty
years ago; that when this Specific Plan Area was approved in 1987, three years prior, a
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 3
Minutes of the Special Meeting  June 26, 2024

new 172-room DoubleTree hotel was built; that, clearly, they envisioned one hotel for the
entire area; that another important point on the proposed 121-room hotel, which has not
been constructed, is that it will make noise and have air impacts as well as impacting the
residents across the street; that the traffic generated by the hotel patrons and the workers,
including the mobile emissions, need to be taken under consideration; that this has not
been analyzed; that regarding entertainment uses, such as amphitheaters, these are
typically considered regional-serving; that many public agencies, including the Office of
Planning and Research, indicate that this warrants an analysis; that the City is asking to
potentially approve an amendment of a speculative use, while it is clear that a real project
is envisioned; and he asked why is the City not considering additional uses, such as
housing.

Christina Sanchez stated that she is a Norwalk resident and a UNITE HERE Local 11
member; that she opposes this item; that they have to make sure that the development
is in the best interest of the City; that it is her understanding that a developer has
expressed an interest in building a hotel and a digital billboard in this area; that this
information has not been disclosed in the report and to the public; that all of the
information should be given to the public in order for the community to make the right
decision; and that consideration should be given as to whether the City needs another
hotel and billboard.

Aracely King stated that she is one of the leaders from UNITE HERE Local 11
representing all the citizens of this City; that she urges the Commission to reject the
amendment of Specific Plan 1 that would allow for another hotel development; that most
of Southern California is experiencing a housing crisis; that there is no need for another
hotel; that the City’s focus should be on creating more housing opportunities, including
affordable housing; that other cities require future hotel projects to enter into a
Development Agreement and that this project lacks such a requirement; that, in
conclusion, amending Specific Plan 1 to accommodate an additional hotel and digital
billboard is not necessary.

In response to Vice Chair Apodaca’s question as to the type of workers that UNITE HERE
Local 11 is representing, Ms. King stated that they are representing all kinds of industry
and hospitality workers, including hotel workers.

Los Angeles resident, Andy Seymour, stated that he, too, is with UNITE HERE Local 11
representing over 30,000 hotel hospitality workers, including some Norwalk residents;
that they strongly oppose the proposal to amend Specific Plan Area No. 1; that Southern
California has a significant housing shortage, not a lack of hotels; that the City should
prioritize and foster housing growth; and that he would ask the Commission to vote “no”.

Since there were no other persons wishing to present testimony, Chair Lopez closed the
public hearing.

Deputy City Attorney Ramirez asked the Director to address some of the issues brought
up.

Director Ramirez shared that the intent of this modification to the Specific Plan is to create
and promote consistency and synergy with the Entertainment District that is going to be
located on the City Hall campus; that this particular Entertainment District project includes
360 residential units, 15 percent of which will be affordable, and 15 percent will be
dedicated for families of veterans; that the City is currently in partnership with Mercy
Housing and will have about 60 units coming on line on Veteran’s Day for families of
veterans; that the City is very aggressive and focused on the development of housing in
general, specifically affordable housing; that regarding the project’s specific component,
they did get a request for a new hotel behind the DoubleTree; that this project has been
in process for almost four years at this point; that in order to move forward with this, there
needs to be a resubmittal; however, the City decided to move forward to help provide
more certainty for development in that area; that there was a sizable office building
contemplated; that they understand that all of the impacts will need to be evaluated during
the specific entitlement project for whatever use comes forward; that, as there are
concerns with providing housing so close to the freeway, they decided to focus the
housing a little further away; that AB 2011, State legislation, went into effect at the
beginning of 2023 that allowed the City to approve a workforce housing project of 76 units
on Front Street; that the intent is to provide more attainable housing for the City’s
workforce and have it combined with the revitalization of historic Front Street.

Vice Chair Apodaca stated that they are very aware of the housing requirements; that
they have been aggressively working on housing projects as the Director just described
in detail; that, in addition to housing, the City also needs revenue to support all of its
residents; that one of the ways to accomplish this is to have a project, such as a hotel;
that as the subject site is next to a freeway, this is not an ideal place for housing; and that
she is intrigued by the testimony given by the Union members, who are representing
hospitality workers, and are opposed to a hotel.

Commissioner Barragan indicated that staff’s comments regarding housing is impressive;
that, as an advocate for homelessness, and an advocate in her professional life for the
Norwalk-La Mirada Unified School District, working with them for the past 24 years, she
knows that this is a big issue, especially affordable housing at all levels; that Norwalk has
been aggressively working towards that goal; that she is comfortable with what Norwalk
is doing to address and accommodate that issue of affordability for families; that, as stated
by staff, the building of housing is a complex issue; and that she is glad that this City is
continuing to work aggressively to address the housing situation.

Director Ramirez shared that, for clarification, the action by the Planning Commission for
the Code amendments are recommendations for consideration by the City Council, and
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 5

that the comments discussed this evening will be part of the record that goes to City
Council for final action.

Chair Lopez stated that the City is taking the housing crisis very seriously; that, as the
Director indicated, Norwalk is one of the first cities to take action with regards to AB 2011;
and that she is proud that the City is being proactive on this matter.

It was moved by Vice Chair Apodaca and seconded by Commissioner Barragan to: (1)
Adopt Resolution No. 24-02 to recommend approval to City Council for Zoning Text
Amendment (ZTA) No. 2024-01; and (2) Consider and find that the project is exempt from
the California Environmental Quality Act pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section
15061(b)(3) (Common Sense Exemption), where it can be seen with certainty there is no
possibility that the activity in question may have significant effect on the environment.

ON ROLL CALL VOTE
AYES: Commissioner Barragan, Commissioner Garcia, Vice Chair Apodaca, and
  Chair Lopez
NOES: None
ABSENT: Commissioner Navas

ZONING TEXT AMENDMENT (ZTA) NO. 2024-02
To amend Title 17 (Zoning), Chapter 17.02, (Approval Procedures) Article I
(Procedure, Hearing, Notices) and Article V (Discretionary Approvals and Permits)
of the Norwalk Municipal Code (NMC) to establish a review process to create a
Special Sign District. Environmental: Consider and find this project to be exempt
from CEQA pursuant to Section15061(b)(3) under the “Common Sense
Exemption”.

Chair Lopez opened the public hearing.

Staff presented the legal requisites for notice of hearing. Consulting Senior Planner
Tatlyan presented a report stating that this is a City initiated project to amend Title 17
(Zoning) to establish a review process to create a Special Sign District, and the associated
environmental determination to consider and find this project to be exempt from CEQA
pursuant to Section 15061(b)(3) under the “Common Sense Exemption” of the California
Code of Regulations; and that staff is recommending that the Commission adopt
Resolution No. 24-03 recommending approval to City Council for Zoning Text
Amendment No. 2024-02 and consider and find that the project is exempt from CEQA
pursuant to Section 15061(b)(3) under the “Common Sense Exemption” of the California
Code of Regulations. Further, she stated that Zoning Text Amendment No. 2024-02
defines the purpose of a Special Sign District, establishes a review process for the
creation of a Special Sign District, clarifies the appropriate review authority and sets
minimum requirements to create a Special Sign District; that, for clarification, a Special
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 6
Minutes of the Special Meeting  June 26, 2024

Sign District is an overlay containing multiple parcels, reasonably grouped together, that
would allow for the approval of a freestanding sign; that with this Code amendment,
businesses have another tool to construct more effective signage through their district
which may allow the signage to be more visible to the freeway or street traffic; that the
proposed Zoning Text Amendment establishes a framework to create a Special Sign
District which is processed similar to a zone change; that any proposed Sign District must
be noticed similar to a zone change and establishes City Council as the appropriate
review authority; that the text amendment also sets the minimum requirements or site
conditions to form a district; that the development standards, in part, state that this applies
only to parcels within Specific Plan Area 1, Specific Plan Area 16, Mixed-use,
Commercial, Institutional and Public Facility Overlay Zone districts; that sign design
guidelines for each district will be reviewed when a Special Sign District request is
received; and that staff finds that the purpose of a Special Sign District aligns with the
goals and policies set forth in the General Plan and will provide economic tools for
businesses to utilize to expand commerce in the City.

Director Ramirez added that the creation of a sign district is a mechanism for future
potential development and requires approval by City Council.

Since there were no persons wishing to present testimony, Chair Lopez closed the public
hearing.

As none of the Commissioners had any comments or questions, it was moved by Vice
Chair Apodaca and seconded by Commissioner Garcia, to: (1) Adopt Resolution No. 24-
03 to recommend approval to City Council for Zoning Text Amendment No. 2024-02; and
(2) Consider and find that the project is exempt from the California Environmental Quality
Act pursuant to Section 15061(b)(3) of the California Code of Regulations, also known as
the “Common Sense Exemption” and Section 15311 (Class 11 – Accessory Structures)
of the California Code of Regulations, for the construction or replacement of minor
accessory structures including on-premise signs.

ON ROLL CALL VOTE
AYES: Commissioner Barragan, Commissioner Garcia, Vice Chair Apodaca, and
  Chair Lopez
NOES: None
ABSENT: Commissioner Navas

ZONING TEXT AMENDMENT (ZTA) NO. 2024-03
To establish Special Sign District No. 01 (SD 1), an overlay for 11 non-residential
properties within the Specific Plan Area 1, Specific Plan Area 16, Institutional and
Public Facility Overlay zone along the Interstate-5 Freeway and amending the
Norwalk Municipal Code to incorporate the development requirements for SD 1.
Environmental: Consider and find that the proposed project is exempt pursuant to
Sections 15061(b)(3) “Common Sense Exemption” and 15311 “Accessory
Structures” of the CEQA Guidelines.

Chair Lopez opened the public hearing.

Staff presented the legal requisites for notice of hearing. Consulting Senior Planner
Tatlyan presented a report stating that this is a City initiated request to establish Special
Sign District No. 01 and the associated environmental determination to consider and find
that the proposed project is exempt pursuant to Sections 15061(b)(3) “Common Sense
Exemption” and 15311 “Accessory Structures” of the California Code of Regulations.
Further, she stated that it is staff’s recommendation that the Planning Commission: (1)
Adopt Resolution No. 24-04 to recommend approval to City Council for Zone Change No.
2024-01; (2) Adopt Resolution No. 24-05 to recommend approval to City Council for
Zoning Text Amendment No. 2024-03; and (3) Consider and find that the project is
exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act pursuant to Section 15061(b)(3) of
the California Code of Regulations, also known as the “Common Sense Exemption” and
Section 15311 (Class 11 – Accessory Structures) of the California Code of Regulations,
for the construction or replacement of minor accessory structures including on-premise
signs.

Continuing with her report, Ms. Tatlyan shared that Special Sign District No. 01 impacts
eleven (11) parcels in Specific Plan Area Nos. 1, 16, and Institutional and Public Facilities
Overlay Zone; that in 2023, City Council adopted the Norwalk Entertainment District –
Civic Center Specific Plan Area No. 16 to advance the City’s goal for the Plan area,
including the Civic Center, as an economic node to enhance the area as a thriving and
experience-oriented center for residents and visitors; that Specific Plan Area No. 1 is a
mixed-use development approved in 1987, located to the south of Specific Plan Area No.
16; that this proposal for Special Sign District No. 01 includes the AMC Theatre, the retail
pad tenants and the Outback Steakhouse; that the DoubleTree Hotel and Sycamore
Village are not included in this proposed district; that there is one existing freestanding
sign located on the Outback Steakhouse property; that the current height of the sign is
70-feet; that the Outback Steakhouse and the City of Norwalk currently have sign panels
on the existing freestanding structure, which was constructed in 1999; and that due to the
freeway expansion and changes to the I-5 Freeway, visibility of the sign has diminished
over time.
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 8

Consulting Senior Planner Tatlyan commented on Zone Change No. 2024-01, stating that
this is a request to establish a C-1 overlay; that the parcels listed in the staff report would
be part of the new Special Sign District No. 01; that establishing this sign district would
provide regulatory relief for the relocation of the existing Outback Steakhouse sign
allowing it to be replaced with a taller, freestanding sign, including other businesses from
the district to be showcased on its sign panels; that Zoning Text Amendment No. 2024-
03 proposes to amend Title 17 (Zoning), Chapter 17.01 (Administration), Article II
(Establishment of Zones, and Limiting the Uses of Land Therein) and Title 17 (Zoning)
Chapter 17.03 (Development Standards), Article III (Signs) of the NMC to establish
development standards for Special Sign District No. 01 and allow one freeway-oriented
freestanding sign up to 100-feet tall; that the proposed sign may be illuminated or non-
illuminated; may have a maximum width of 30 feet, and may have a maximum number of
six (6) sign panels for up to six (6) tenants; that, at this time, there is no implementing
project for Sign District No. 01; that any future signs associated with invoking Sign District
No. 01 would require the review and approval of the Planning Commission subject to a
Sign Use Permit; that staff finds that Special Sign District No. 01 aligns with the goals and
policies set forth in the General Plan, and will provide additional economic tools for the
businesses to utilize and expand commerce; that, as she stated at the beginning of the
staff report, based on the analysis, staff recommends that the Planning Commission: (1)
adopt Resolution No. 24-04 recommending approval to City Council for Zone Change No.
2024-01; (2) Adopt Resolution No. 24-05 recommending approval to City Council for
Zoning Text Amendment No. 2024-03; and (3) Consider and find that the project is
exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act pursuant to Section 15061(b)(3) of
the California Code of Regulations, also known as the “Common Sense Exemption” and
Section 15311 (Class 11 – Accessory Structures) of the California Code of Regulations,
for the construction or replacement of minor accessory structures including on-premise
signs.

In response to Vice Chair Apodaca’s request for clarification if the DoubleTree Hotel
signage is part of this proposal, Ms. Tatlyan replied that it is not. Director Ramirez added
that they are working with DoubleTree and the Water District to relocate their existing
freeway sign that identifies the DoubleTree, Sonoma Grill and AMC Theatres as the sign
needs to be enhanced, made a little bit taller and updated so that it provides better
visibility for those uses.

Jordan Sisson, representing UNITE HERE Local 11, thanked staff for their presentation.
He stated that he would like to know when these three public hearings are going to the
City Council for their consideration; that he wants to make sure that his office is on the
City’s notification list on behalf of their client, UNITE HERE Local 11, and that he also
wants to make sure that the Director and City Attorney have hard copies of his letter which
should be forwarded to the City Clerk.
 Norwalk Planning Commission  Page 9

Director Ramirez thanked Mr. Sisson for the hard copies. He stated that he will make
sure that the hard copies are distributed; and that the anticipated City Council date is July
16, 2024.

In response to Chair Lopez’ question if staff wished to make a rebuttal statement, Director
Ramirez stated that regarding the Special Sign District, the City Council’s goal is to
promote all the businesses in the City and specifically promote and identify certain regions
that have a lot of economic potential; that with the work on Economic Development Node
1, the Entertainment District, this is part of that effort to provide higher visibility to all the
businesses going from the Outback, DoubleTree, AMC Theatres and the new businesses
that will eventually be built on the City Hall campus.

Since there were no other persons wishing to present testimony, Chair Lopez closed the
public hearing.

As none of the Planning Commissioners voiced any comments on the item, it was moved
by Vice Chair Apodaca and seconded by Commissioner Barragan, to: (1) Adopt
Resolution No. 24-04 recommending approval to City Council for Zone Change No. 2024-
01; (2) Adopt Resolution No. 24-05 recommending approval to City Council for Zoning
Text Amendment No. 2024-03; and (3) Consider and find that the project is exempt from
the California Environmental Quality Act pursuant to Section 15061(b)(3) of the California
Code of Regulations, also known as the “Common Sense Exemption” and Section 15311
(Class 11 – Accessory Structures) of the California Code of Regulations, for the
construction or replacement of minor accessory structures including on-premise signs.

GENERAL PLAN AMENDMENT (GPA) NO. 2022-01 (2024-01)

ZONING TEXT AMENDMENT (ZTA) NO. 2022-02 (2024-04) TO ESTABLISH
SPECIFIC PLAN NO. 17, THE “NORWALK TRANSIT VILLAGE SPECIFIC PLAN”
FINAL ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT REPORT (FEIR) SCH NO. 2022070103
City of Norwalk (“Applicant”); a request to establish a specific plan to allow a mixed-use
development with up to 66,647 square feet of neighborhood commercial uses, 13,500
square feet of active commercial uses, 770 residential units (40% of the units will be
designated as “affordable”), and 3.7 acres of open space. The project site consists of
approximately 32.3 acres situated between Imperial Highway to the north, Zimmerman

INTRODUCTION/BACKGROUND:

The Density Bonus Ordinance was adopted by Ordinance No. 14-1656 in 2014, in order for
the NMC to be in compliance with the requirements of State Density Bonus Law by
establishing consistent objectives, policies, regulations, development and design standards,
and review criteria for implementing density bonus requirements.

The City’s 6th Cycle Housing Element Update (HEU), adopted in February 2023, lists
Program 1.5 (Density Bonus), which requires the City to update the existing density bonus
ordinance for compliance with State law. The amended ordinance aligns the City’s
regulations with State requirements and enhances the effectiveness of the density bonus
program in promoting affordable housing development in Norwalk.

Additionally, the City’s 6th Cycle HEU Program 3.6 (Definition of Family) requires the City to
amend the current definition of “family” to ensure it is inclusive, non-discriminatory, and does
not exclude any uses.

requirements, ensuring compliance and promoting affordable housing development
consistent with the City’s Housing Element Update goals.

While the adoption of the density bonus ordinance would bring the City into compliance with
State Density Bonus laws, it also incentivizes the development of affordable housing by
allowing developers to build more units than typically permitted under the City’s zoning
regulations. While density bonus is an important incentive, other factors such as land value,
project economics, land cost, and labor and materials are also important in determining the
feasibility of a development.

The updated definition of “Family” ensures inclusivity, removes discriminatory language, and
broadens the definition to accommodate various uses.

Zoning Text Amendment

SUMMARY:

The proposed ZTA No. 2024-05, which involves repealing and replacing the current density
bonus ordinance from the NMC, will bring the current ordinance into compliance with the
requirements of State Density Bonus Law.

The new density bonus ordinance will retain the current purpose and applicability statements;
update eligibility and procedural requirements; add comprehensive requirements for
calculating density bonus requirements and corresponding required incentives and
reductions; modify the density bonus housing agreement and development standard
provisions; and revise the list of definitions to be consistent with requirements of State law.

Additionally, the amendment to the Review Authority Table is required to be consistent with
the amendments to the density bonus ordinance. The density bonus ordinance is of critical
importance for the City to be in compliance with State law requirements.

Lastly, the modification of the definition of “Family” is required to comply with Housing Element
Program 3.6 (Definition of Family). Therefore, Staff recommends that the Planning
Commission recommend approval of the project to City Council.

§ 17.04.400 Density bonus.
A. Purpose. It is the purpose of this section to encourage the production of very low-, low-, and
  moderate-income housing units, senior citizens housing units, provisions of childcare facilities,
  student housing units, and donations of land in accordance with Government Code Sections 65915
  through 65918, as may be amended from time to time ("State Density Bonus Law"). In enacting this
  section, it is also the intent of the City to facilitate the development of affordable housing and to
  implement the goals, objectives, and policies of the housing element of the City's General Plan.

B. Definitions. Whenever the following terms are used in this section, they shall have the meaning
  established:

  "Affordable rent" as defined in Health and Safety Code Section 50053(b).

  "Affordable sales price" means a sales price at which very low-, low-, or moderate-income
  households can qualify for the purchase of target units, calculated in accordance with Health and
  Safety Code Section 50052.5 and the regulations adopted by the California Department of Housing
  and Community Development.

  “Base density” means the maximum allowable gross residential density permitted under this Title and
  the Land Use Element of the General Plan or any specific plan applicable to the proposed
  development, as of the date of application submittal by the applicant to the City. If the underlying
  zoning district is inconsistent with the base density allowed under the Land Use Element of the
  General Plan, the greater shall prevail.

  “Base project” means the proposed housing development before any extra density is added through
  the State Density Bonus Law in accordance with all local regulations, without including any bonus
  units, concessions, or waivers.

  “Base unit” means only those units permitted by the underlying zoning regulations, excluding any
  units added through a density bonus awarded pursuant to this section or any other provisions of the
  Norwalk Municipal Code granting a greater density bonus.

  “Commercial project” means a development that includes commercial uses like retail, office, or
  industrial spaces, and may also apply to mixed-use developments.

  "Concession" shall have the same meaning as the term "incentive" defined herein.

  "Density bonus" means a density increase of up to those percentages specified in the State Density
  Bonus Law above the otherwise maximum residential density under the applicable zoning
  designation on the date the application is deemed complete.

SUBJECT: Accessory Dwelling Unit Ordinance Update Study Session Workshop

BACKGROUND:

Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) is accessory to a primary residence and provides
complete independent living facilities for one or more persons and is located on a lot with
a proposed or existing primary residential unit. The configuration of an ADU varies as
follows:
  • Detached: The unit is separated from the primary structure.
  • Attached: The unit is attached to the primary structure.
  • Converted Existing Space: Existing floor area (e.g., master bedroom, attached
  garage, storage area, or similar use, or an accessory structure) on the lot of the
  primary residence that is converted into an independent living unit.
  • Junior Accessory Dwelling Unit (JADU): A specific type of conversion of existing
  space that is contained entirely within an existing or proposed single-family
  residence.

Since 2003, the California Legislature has adopted numerous laws governing ADUs and
JADU’s to limit local regulations and incentivize the construction of ADUs and JADUs.
The increase construction of ADUs is part of the State’s overall strategy to address a
Statewide housing crisis and to increase market rate and affordable housing unit supply.
ADUs are typically smaller than the average home in a community, they tend to be more
affordable than other market-rate units, thereby better serving lower income households.

The Norwalk Municipal Code (NMC) was last updated in 2018 to comply with ADU State
laws at that time. The 2018 NMC update included use restrictions, location requirements
and development standards for ADUs, but is mostly out of compliance with current State
law. While the ADU standards adopted in 2018 have been out of compliance with State
laws, staff has been applying the State ADU standards for proposed ADUs as required.

ANALYSIS:

Under the current NMC ADU development standards adopted in 2018, one ADU, ranging
from 400 to 720 sq. ft. in size, is permitted on properties developed as single-family
residences in the R-1, R-2, R-3, and R-4, and R-H zones. Development standards include
minimum lot width, size, and primary dwelling size requirements. Property owners are
required to live on the property constructed with an ADU.

Changes to ADU Laws

Since the City’s adoption of the ADU ordinance in 2018, there have been additional State
ADU bills passed between 2019 to 2024, which are listed as follows: AB 68, 345, 587,
670, 671, 881, 2221, 2533, and SB 13, 477, 897, 1077 and 1211 (Government Code
sections 66310 to 66342). Some of these bills were part of the 2019 legislative ADU
housing package. Some bills are in effect and some will be effective beginning January
1, 2025. The most significant provisions of these bills are summarized below:

  •  ADU application review times.
  •  Elimination of owner-occupancy restrictions for ADUs.
  •  The sale/conveyance of ADUs.
  •  Introduction of JADUs, ADUs in multi-family properties, and a statewide exemption
  ADUs (Exempt ADU) and development standards for these types of ADUs.
  •  Standards for conversion of existing accessory buildings into ADUs.
  •  ADUs required to permitted in zones where residential uses are permitted
  (including mixed-use zones).
  •  Prohibition of lot coverage limits and minimum lot size requirements.
  •  Minimum and maximum standards for floor area, setbacks, and height.
  •  Off-street parking requirements and replacement.

Junior Accessory Dwelling Units, ADUs in Multiple-Family properties, and Exempt ADUs

Currently, the City’s ADU ordinance does not include standards for the development of
JADUs, ADUs for Multiple-Family Residential properties, and Exempt ADUs. As part of
the updates to the ADU ordinance, development standards for the aforementioned types
of ADUs are necessary to conform to the State ADU bills.

JADU

Currently, the NMC does not have provisions for JADUs. As previously mentioned, a
JADU is a specific type of conversion of existing space that is contained entirely within an
existing or proposed single-family residence.

Listed below are the State required JADU development standards that will be
incorporated into the City’s ADU Ordinance update:

  1. Must be contained entirely within a single-family residence.
  2. May include separate sanitation facilities or may share sanitation facilities
  with the existing single-family residence.
  3. Must have independent entrance from primary dwelling.
  4. Size: 150 sq. ft. minimum to 500 sq. ft. maximum.
  5. Owner occupancy covenant required.
  6. May not be sold or conveyed separately.
  7. Short term rental prohibited.

ADUs on Properties Developed with Multiple Family Dwellings

Currently, the NMC does not have development standards for ADUs on properties
developed with multi-family dwellings. For the purposes of State ADU Law, a structure
with two or more attached dwellings on a single lot is considered a multifamily dwelling
structure. Under the States ADU bills, the City is required to allow the following ADU
configurations:

  1. Attached ADUs, subject to all the following:
  • Location. Multiple ADUs within portions of existing multiple-family structures that
  are not used as livable space, including, but not limited to, storage rooms, boiler
  rooms, passageways, attics, basements, or garages, provided each unit complies
  with state building standards for dwellings.
  • Number. ADUs equal to a maximum of 25 percent of the existing dwelling units,
  with a minimum of one ADU.

  2. Detached ADUs, subject to all the following:
  • Location. Within an existing or proposed accessory building.
  • Number. Existing properties - Up to eight detached ADUs or as many detached
  ADUs as there are primary units on the lot, whichever is less). Proposed Multi-
  Family Dwellings – Two ADUs.
  • Setbacks. The minimum interior side yard and rear yard setbacks shall be four
  feet.
